en.content:
Tai Po’s fire inquiry has surfaced a familiar but uncomfortable question for Hong Kong: when safety fails, who truly had the power—and the responsibility—to stop it. The report that owners’ corporation members tried to discourage the use of flammable boards and substandard construction nets, even while the broader renovation proceeded, suggests not a single, neat villain but a chain of decisions shaped by cost, timelines, and risk. Independent inquiries do not absolve anyone, but they can clarify how pressure and procedure—rather than mere negligence—combine to turn warnings into tragedy.

At the heart of this case is the governance of building works, where multiple parties share influence yet accountability can blur. Owners’ corporations manage collective decisions, contractors execute technical choices, and regulators set the rules that define compliance. When the inquiry hears that warnings were made yet problematic materials still featured in the project, it raises concerns about whether Hong Kong’s system adequately empowers “stop” points—clear contractual duties, enforceable inspection standards, and effective escalation mechanisms when safety concerns arise. In other words, it is not enough to ask whether someone objected; we must ask whether objections were structurally able to change outcomes.

There is also a wider social implication. Hong Kong residents have long lived with the reality that property maintenance and redevelopment involve bargaining between affordability and safety. The Tai Po case underscores that the margin for compromise is narrow where fire risks are concerned. If lessons are to matter, public confidence will depend on concrete reforms: stricter enforcement of fire-related specifications, transparent reporting of inspections for major works, and clearer liability for every party who either ignored or failed to act upon safety red flags. At the same time, fairness requires the investigation to avoid turning the story into a simplistic moral drama; systemic weaknesses must be identified alongside individual conduct.

Ultimately, the inquiry should push the city toward a culture where safety is treated as a condition of proceeding, not an afterthought to be negotiated away. Hong Kong has the institutions to improve standards—what is needed is the will to tighten incentives, reduce grey areas in responsibility, and ensure that when residents or managers flag hazards, the system responds with effective authority. Only then can the promise of accountability translate into practical protection for future communities.

zh.content:
泰入王福閣大火調查入面，最叫人唔舒服嘅位，唔係單一個人失誤，而係業主立案法團、裝修承辦商同樓宇安全之間嗰套「互相推責」機制。新聞提到業主立案法團曾經反對使用可燃物料、亦曾就施工網等問題表達關注，聽落似乎「有人做好咗自己份內事」。但調查更重要嘅含意係：就算立案法團有疑慮，若最後冇有效制止、冇即時升級處理、冇用硬措施守住安全門檻（包括停工、要求合規文件、確立責任鏈），就算口頭上「盡咗力」，現場結果仍然係悲劇落地。呢種「半推半就」正正令公眾覺得制度性風險被輕描淡寫。

同時，今次亦逼人思考：樓宇管理唔應只靠程序、仲要靠問責。業主立案法團作為法定機構，若得出「相對應該」但未能「肯定可承擔」嘅判斷，就容易陷入灰色地帶——一邊要配合業權運作，另一邊又唔願承擔全面否決或法律後果。結果就會變成「爭取降低麻煩」而唔係「爭取消除危險」。香港社會常見嘅另一個痛點亦浮現：當事故發生後先至啟動調查，公眾往往更想見到事前監管同風險管理嘅力度，而唔係只得事後解釋「當時已經反對」。

政府若要回應民意，核心唔係只聽取各方陳述，而係要重新校準政策落地嘅最低標準：包括對涉及可燃/危險材料嘅改建工程，強化審批同現場核實；對承辦商同相關文件設定更清晰嘅責任追溯；以及令業主立案法團面對安全風險時，真係有權、有指引、亦有配套去作出「即時制止」決定。否則，下一次即使再有人「拚咗最大努力」，仍可能只係重演同一套結構性失靈。

立場上，我認為今次最大警號係：安全唔可以變成「可選擇」嘅成本。消防、建築合規同工程材料嘅要求，根本就唔應該靠各方心情去平衡。真正應被追究嘅，係喺事故之前能否做到有效阻斷風險、以及系統如何確保每個環節唔可以用程序拖延責任。當災民用生命換嚟嘅教訓被淡化，社會就只會越來越難相信制度會保護普通人。希望今次調查唔止係追溯過往，更要改寫未來。
